items.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: And Harry Lim, the jazz critic from Batavia Java by way of Holland was living in Chicago at the time. And he and I went every night to hear Ellington.

ctx.x: You just started to touch on a subject that I find interesting and that is the racial thing that was happening at that time, with this music and the fans, and how did that kind of balance —

Very, very heartbreaking in a way, but somehow I mean as you look back it was terrible, but it was a given. And I was interviewed by somebody from the Black Entertainment Network, she came to my house. And she said, “you don’t look like a jazz groupie, to be following the band.” Well boy I was. I was the first jazz groupie. I mean I’d hear Ellington was playing in Rock Island, Illinois, and if I wasn’t doing anything that day, I’d get on the train and just go and hear the band. So I heard him quite a lot. They…

really kind of bad. But I remember a few moments of anxiety. Lee Wiley was living in the Rockefeller Apartments, not far from where we are now. And it’s kind of a tony building. I don’t know if they called it the Rockefeller Apartments, but it’s across from the Museum of Modern Art. And she had invited the gang from Nick’s to come over. And she suddenly said, “[gasps] Zutty Singleton — they won’t let him through the lobby.” And I said, “let me handle this.” And my mother was sort of a Grand Dame and she’d “brook…
